title: The fortunes of human societies

paragraphs.text: In an effort to understand the reasons why some past societies collapsed completely, while others survived, and to draw tentative conclusions regarding the present, I have arrived at a five-point framework of important factors. In any particular case four of those factors – environmental damage, climate change, hostile neighbors, and friendly trade partners – may or may not prove significant. However, the fifth – a society's responses to its problems – is always crucial.

The damage that people inadvertently inflict on their environment is one potential factor affecting a society's destiny. The extent and reversibility of that damage depend partly on characteristics of people, for example, how many trees they cut down per acre per year, and partly on characteristics of the environment, for example, characteristics determining how many seedlings germinate per acre of land, and how rapidly saplings grow. Hence the reasons why only certain societies suffered environmental collapses might in principle involve either the exceptional carelessness of people, the exceptional fragility of some aspects of the environment, or both.

A next consideration in my five-point framework is climate change, a term that today we tend to associate with global warming caused by humans. In fact, climates may also change because of changes in natural forces, such as the amount of heat put out by the sun, volcanic eruptions that inject dust into the atmosphere, the orientation of the Earth's axis with respect to its orbit, and the distribution of land and ocean over the face of the Earth. Frequently discussed cases of natural climate change include the advance and retreat of continental ice sheets during the Ice Ages beginning over two million years ago, the so-called Little Ice Age from about A.D. 1400 to 1800, and the global cooling following the enormous volcanic eruption of Indonesia's Mount Tambora in 1815.

A third consideration is hostile neighbors. All but a few historical societies have been geographically close enough to other societies to have had at least some contact with them. Relations with neighboring societies may be intermittently or chronically hostile. A society may be able to hold off its enemies as long as it is strong, only to succumb when it becomes weakened for any reason. The immediate cause of the collapse will then be military conquest, but the ultimate cause will have been the factor that caused the weakening. Hence collapses for ecological or other reasons often masquerade as military defeats.

The most familiar debate in this respect involves the fall of the Western Roman Empire. Rome became increasingly beset by barbarian invasions, with the conventional date for the Empire's fall being taken somewhat arbitrarily as A.D. 476, the year in which the last emperor of the West was deposed. However, even before the rise of the Roman Empire, there had been 'barbarian' tribes who periodically attacked the civilizations of Mediterranean Europe, as well as those of China and India. For over a thousand years, Rome had successfully held off the barbarians, but eventually, it was the barbarians rather than Romans who won the battles.

What was the fundamental reason for that shift in fortune? Was it because of changes in the barbarians themselves, such that they became more numerous or better organized, or acquired better weapons or more horses, or profited from climate change in the Central Asian steppes? Or was it instead that the barbarians were always waiting on the Roman Empire's frontiers, and that they couldn't prevail until Rome became weakened by internal problems? In that case we would blame Rome's fall on its own problems, with the barbarians just providing the decisive blow. Essentially the same question has been debated for the fall of the Khmer Empire centered on Angkor Wat in relation to invasions by Thai neighbors, for the decline in the Harappan Indus Valley civilization in relation to Aryan invasions, and for the fall of Mycenaean Greece and other Bronze Age Mediterranean societies.

The fourth factor is the converse of the third set: decreased support from friendly neighbors, as opposed to increased attacks by hostile neighbors. All but a few historical societies have had friendly trade partners as well as neighboring enemies. Often, the partner and the enemy are one and the same neighbor, whose behavior shifts back and forth between friendly and hostile. Most societies depend to some extent on friendly neighbors, either for imports of essential trade goods, like U.S. imports of oil, and Japanese imports of wood, and seafood, or else for cultural ties that lend cohesion to the society, such as Australia's cultural identity being largely imported from Britain in the 18th century. Hence the risk arises that, if your trade partner becomes weakened for any reason and can no longer supply the essential import or the cultural tie, your own society may become weakened as a result.

The last factor in my five-point framework involves the question of the society's responses to its problems, whatever those problems are. Different societies respond differently to similar problems. For instance, problems of deforestation arose for many past societies, among which Highland New Guinea, Japan, and Tonga developed successful forest management and continued to prosper, while Easter Island and Norse Greenland failed to develop successful forest management, and collapsed as a result. How can we understand such differing outcomes? A society's responses depend on its political, economic, and social institutions and on its cultural values, and these affect whether the society solves, or even tries to solve, its problems.

groups.title: The fall of the Western Roman Empire
content: Barbarians eventually overcame the Romans in the 5th century, after the latter had been under attack for a very long period. The interesting question is why the barbarians experienced {{31}} on this occasion. One hypothesis is that they had gained in strength. For example, they may have increased in {{32}} , have built up greater {{33}} , or benefited from a change in climate. Another hypothesis is that the Romans had developed {{34}} , so they were more vulnerable to attack. This would then be the fundamental {{35}} of the fall of the Roman Empire. Whatever the reason, the same question about the fall of the Roman Empire applies to the disappearance of several other historical societies.
